title: Word Frequency
oneLiner: Count how many times each word appears using a dictionary, treating upper and lower case as the same word.
keyTakeaway: The counting idiom: for each item, add 1 to its entry, starting it at 0 the first time. In C# use counts[w] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(w) + 1; in Python counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1, or collections.Counter.
explanation:
Given a line of text made of letters and spaces, return a dictionary mapping each word, in lowercase, to the number of times it appears. "Go go GO" gives {"go": 3}. Extra spaces don't create empty words, and text with no words gives an empty dictionary.

Lowercase the text, split it into words (Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries) in C#, split() in Python), and count with a dictionary. The tricky part is the first time you see a word: reading a missing key throws (KeyNotFoundException, KeyError). Either check first (ContainsKey / in), or read with a fallback of 0: counts.GetValueOrDefault(word) + 1 in C#, counts.get(word, 0) + 1 in Python.

Python's standard library has this built in: collections.Counter(words) counts everything in one call, and dict(Counter(words)) turns it into a plain dictionary. In C#, LINQ can do it in one expression: words.GroupBy(w => w).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count()). Write the loop version first. The order of keys in your dictionary doesn't matter to the tests.

visualizationSteps.message: The words, already lowercased and split. Start with an empty dictionary.
"pump" is new: it starts from 0 and becomes 1.
"fan" is new: it starts from 0 and becomes 1.
"pump" is already a key: add 1, now 2.
"valve" is new: it starts from 0 and becomes 1.
"pump" is already a key: add 1, now 3.

complexity.note: Lowercasing and splitting the n characters is O(n), and each word costs one O(1) average dictionary update (plus hashing the word, which is covered by the O(n) characters). The words and the dictionary take O(n) space.
